text:
The three days of travel lie in the passage like a suspended sentence. Outwardly nothing happens; in significance everything has happened. The servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire are carefully named; the instruments of the act are before us before the act itself occurs. Obedience and horror remain joined in the narrative, and neither prevails. Faith, in Genesis 22, appears as an ordered relation, a disposition of persons and commands, rather than as a feeling.

Placed beside the earlier promise, the scene loses part of its apparent distance from it. Isaac is the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; that promise is now made the matter of a test. The single word is hineni, rendered "here I am," and Abraham speaks it three times: to God, to Isaac, and to the angel. In each place it bears another weight; with each repetition it costs him more. Presence has become the speech of loss in Abraham.
